mechanism.description: Patients with prior symptomatic coronary disease or symptomatic heart failure will on average derive LESS incremental benefit from intensive SBP control (<120 mmHg) than patients without prior CVD because: (1) a higher proportion of their events are due to fixed atherosclerosis or structural pump failure that respond less to short-term BP lowering, and (2) they have greater susceptibility to hypotension-related ischemia or decompensation (increasing harms and reducing delivered intensity). The attenuation is expected to be greatest for recent ischemic events or active heart failure and smaller for remote, stable atherosclerosis. This interaction is moderated by frailty, timing of CVD (recent vs remote), and concurrent cardioprotective therapies (statin/antiplatelet use) which may change the preventable fraction.

mechanism.description: Patients with mild-to-moderate CKD (eGFR ~45	6, ACR <300 mg/g) are likely to derive GREATER absolute cardiovascular benefit from intensive SBP lowering because they have higher baseline rates of stroke and HF that are pressure-sensitive and because moderate BP lowering reduces these events. In contrast, patients with advanced CKD (eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73m2) or heavy albuminuria (ACR 300 mg/g) are more prone to AKI and sustained GFR decline when perfusion pressure is lowered; these renal harms can force dose reductions or cessation and increase competing morbidity, attenuating net benefit or producing net harm. The direction and magnitude of the treatment effect therefore depend on eGFR and albuminuria levels and on how renal adverse events are managed.
